title: Your first commit
objectives: Turn a folder into a Git repository
Stage a file with git add and commit it
Predict what git status reports after each step

screens.prose:
Your Stage 0 folder holds `returns.py` and `README.md`. You turn it into a Git project whose first branch is `main`, and ask Git what it sees:

```sh
$ cd ~/stage0
$ git init -b main
Initialized empty Git repository in /Users/ana/stage0/.git/
$ git status
On branch main
No commits yet
Untracked files:
        README.md
        returns.py
```

Without `-b main`, many setups name the branch `master`.

params.label: Working folder, staging area and repository

state.caption: Each card is a change to a file. The files themselves stay in your working folder.

screens.question: What has Git saved so far?

options.text: Nothing yet: both files are untracked
Both files, as a first snapshot
options.why: You took `git init` as a save. It only creates an empty repository, the hidden `.git` folder.

options.text: `returns.py` only, because it is code
options.why: Git treats every file alike. It saves nothing until you choose files and commit them.

hints.text: Read the reply to `git init`. What word describes the repository?
Both cards are still in the working folder.
The repository is empty, and status says No commits yet. Untracked means Git is not keeping that file.

feedback.correct: Nothing is saved yet. `git init` made an empty repository.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read what `git init` and `git status` reported.

explain.text: `git init` created an empty **repository**, the hidden `.git` folder where Git will keep the history. Your two files are **untracked**: Git sees them but keeps no copy. Choosing what to keep is the next step.

screens.prose:
Git has three places. You edit files in the **working folder**. The repository holds the commits. Between them sits a third place. You type:

```sh
$ git add returns.py
```

params.label: Working folder, staging area and repository

state.caption: Each card is a change to a file. The files themselves stay in your working folder.

screens.question: Drag each card to where you think it is now.

hints.text: The command names one file. Does adding make a commit?
This is the card the command names.
returns.py moves to the staging area. README.md was not named, so it stays put.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move only the file the command names, and only one step.

byKey.ret: `git add` does not make a commit. It puts returns.py in the staging area, waiting for the next commit.
byKey.readme: You moved README.md too. The command named only returns.py.

explain.text: `git add returns.py` put that file in the **staging area**: the list of changes the next commit will hold. Nothing is in the repository yet. README.md is still untracked.

screens.prose:
Now you make the commit. `-m` gives it a message in quotes:

```sh
$ git commit -m "Add daily returns script"
```

params.label: Working folder, staging area and repository

state.caption: Each card is a change to a file. The files themselves stay in your working folder.

screens.question: Drag each card to where it is after the commit.

hints.text: A commit takes what is waiting in the staging area. What is waiting there?
This is the only staged card.
returns.py goes into the repository. README.md was never added, so it stays in the working folder.

feedback.correct: The staged change went into the repository as the first commit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A commit takes everything staged, and nothing else.

byKey.readme: You committed README.md too. A commit takes only what is staged, and README.md was never added.
byKey.ret: The commit takes everything in the staging area into the repository. Nothing staged stays behind.

explain.text: The commit took the staged returns.py into the **repository** as a snapshot. README.md was not staged, so it is not in the commit. Working folder, staging area, repository: these are Git's three places.

screens.prose: Git confirmed the commit, `[main (root-commit) 3f9a2c1]`, and reported 1 file changed. Then you run `git status` again.

params.label: Working folder, staging area and repository

state.caption: Each card is a change to a file. The files themselves stay in your working folder.

screens.question: What does `git status` report now?

options.text: Untracked files: `README.md`
nothing to commit, working tree clean
options.why: You forgot README.md. It was never added, so Git still lists it as untracked.

options.text: Changes to be committed: `returns.py`
options.why: That was true before the commit. The commit took the staged change into the repository.

options.text: Untracked files: `README.md` and `returns.py`
options.why: returns.py is in a commit now, so Git tracks it. Only README.md is untracked.

hints.text: Which card is still outside the repository?
This card was never staged.
returns.py is committed and unchanged. README.md was never added, so it is still untracked.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at where each card is now.

explain.text: returns.py is committed and unchanged, so `git status` has nothing to say about it. README.md was never added, so it is listed as untracked. `git status` reports only what differs.

screens.prose: You fix a sign error in `returns.py` and save it. A new card appears: the change you have not committed. Then you run `git status`.

params.label: Working folder, staging area and repository

state.caption: Each card is a change to a file. The files themselves stay in your working folder.

screens.question: Under which heading does `git status` list `returns.py`?

options.text: Changes not staged for commit: modified: `returns.py`
Untracked files: `returns.py`
options.why: returns.py is in a commit, so Git tracks it. An edited tracked file shows as modified, not untracked.

options.text: Changes to be committed: modified: `returns.py`
options.why: You took saving as staging. Only `git add` stages a change.

options.text: It is not listed: the file was committed
options.why: Saving changed the file. Git compares it with the last commit and sees the difference.

hints.text: Which place is the new card in?
The new change sits in the working folder.
Git tracks returns.py, and the file differs from the commit. The change is not staged yet.

feedback.correct: A tracked file with an unstaged edit is listed as modified, not staged.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the file is tracked, and whether the edit is staged.

explain.text: Git compared your working copy with the last commit and found the fix. Because you have not run `git add`, the change is **not staged**. Saving a file never stages it.

screens.prose:
You are in a hurry. You skip `git add` and type:

```sh
$ git commit -m "Fix sign error in returns"
```

params.label: Working folder, staging area and repository

state.caption: Each card is a change to a file. The files themselves stay in your working folder.

screens.question: What happens?

options.text: No commit is made, because nothing is staged
A new commit holding the fixed `returns.py`
options.why: You expected commit to take every edit. It takes only what is staged, and nothing is.

options.text: A new commit holding both files
options.why: You expected commit to sweep up the whole folder. It reads only the staging area, which is empty.

options.text: A new commit with the message and no changes
options.why: Git refuses to make a commit when nothing is staged.

hints.text: Where does a commit take its changes from?
This place is empty.
The staging area is empty, so there is nothing to commit. Git says no changes added to commit.

feedback.correct: Git prints "no changes added to commit" and makes nothing.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at what is in the staging area.

byKey.fixed: You expected the commit to pick up your saved fix. The fix is not staged, so the commit has nothing to take.
byKey.all: You treated commit as saving the folder. It records only staged changes, and none are staged.

explain.text: A commit reads the staging area and nothing else. It was empty, so Git printed "no changes added to commit" and made nothing. Run `git add returns.py` first, then commit.

screens.prose:
You also jotted ideas in a new file, `notes.txt`. Then you stage with a dot, which means this whole folder:

```sh
$ git add .
```

params.label: Working folder, staging area and repository

state.caption: Each card is a change to a file. The files themselves stay in your working folder.

screens.question: Drag each card to where it is after `git add .`.

hints.text: Which changes in the working folder does the dot cover?
All three of these are in the working folder.
The dot stages every change in the folder, tracked or untracked. The committed card does not move.

feedback.correct: All three changes are staged, the notes included.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The dot means every change in this folder.

byKey.notes: notes.txt is new, but the dot covers new files too. It is staged with the rest.
byKey.readme: README.md was untracked, and the dot stages untracked files too.
byKey.ret2: The sign fix is a change in this folder, so the dot stages it.
byKey.ret: That card is already committed. Staging never touches the repository.

explain.text: `git add .` staged every change in the folder, including your scratch notes. That is quick, and it is how unwanted files sneak into commits. Next lesson shows how to stage exactly what you mean.

screens.prose:
Every commit follows the same cycle. Edit in the working folder, stage with `git add`, record with `git commit`:

```sh
$ git add returns.py
$ git commit -m "Fix sign error in returns"
$ git status
```
screens.question: Where does `git commit` take its changes from?

options.text: The staging area
The working folder
options.why: You expected commit to read your folder. You saw an unstaged fix left out entirely.

options.text: The repository
options.why: The repository is where the commit goes, not where it comes from.

hints.text: When you skipped `git add`, why was nothing committed?
The commit had nothing to take, because the staging area was empty.

feedback.correct: A commit records exactly what is staged.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall the commit that never happened.

explain.text: You saw a commit take the staged card and leave README.md behind. You saw a commit refuse when nothing was staged. `git add` chooses; `git commit` records.

screens.prose: Your Stage 0 project in `~/stage0` has `returns.py`, which reads `prices.csv` and prints daily returns. A fresh terminal opens in your home folder. You want a history that starts with the script alone.

params.label: Working folder, staging area and repository

screens.question: Put the commands in order.

lines.text: `git commit -m "Compute daily returns from closing prices"`
`git status`, to check what is left

hints.text: Which folder must the terminal be in before `git init`?
Move into the project, create the repository, stage the script, commit it, then check.

feedback.correct: Into the folder, create the repository, stage, commit, check.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each command needs the one before it to have run.

explain.text: `cd` comes first, or `git init` makes a repository in your home folder. Staging must come before committing. The final `git status` shows `prices.csv` still untracked; the next lesson tells Git to ignore it.

ideas: `git init` makes an empty repository. Nothing is saved until you commit.
`git add` puts a change in the staging area; `git commit` records everything staged, and nothing else.
`git status` lists what differs: staged changes, unstaged changes and untracked files.

formula.name: The commit cycle
formula.note: Saving a file moves nothing. Only these two commands do.

summary.trap: `git commit` without `git add` records nothing. Saving a file does not stage it.

quiz.prose: On a new laptop, your first `git commit` stops with: "Please tell me who you are."
quiz.question: Why does Git need this?

options.text: Every commit records its author's name and email
Git must log in to GitHub before it can commit
options.why: Commits are made on your machine. No account or network is involved.

options.text: The folder is not a repository yet
options.why: Then Git would say "not a git repository". This message is about you, not the folder.

feedback.correct: A commit records who made it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall what a commit records.

explain.text: Each commit stores an author. Set yours once with `git config --global user.name "Ana Silva"` and the same for `user.email`. After that, commits work.

quiz.prose: In a new repository with no commits, you run `git add signal.py`. The folder also holds `backtest.py`, never added.
quiz.question: What does `git status` list under Changes to be committed?

options.text: new file: `signal.py`
new file: `signal.py` and new file: `backtest.py`
options.why: You staged the whole folder in your head. Only the file you named is staged.

options.text: Nothing, because there are no commits yet
options.why: Staging works before the first commit too. signal.py is waiting for it.

feedback.correct: Only the named file is staged.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. `git add` stages only what you name.

explain.text: `git add signal.py` staged that one file, so it is listed as a new file to be committed. backtest.py stays under Untracked files.

quiz.prose:
In a repository with nothing staged, you edit `a.py` and run:

```sh
$ git add a.py
$ git commit -m "First change"
$ git commit -m "Second change"
```
quiz.question: How many new commits does this make?

widget.label: New commits
widget.accept: 1: the second commit has nothing staged.

feedback.correct: One. The second commit found nothing staged.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what is staged before each commit.

byKey.two: You counted both commit commands. The first emptied the staging area, so the second had nothing to record.
byKey.zero: The first commit had a.py staged, so it succeeded.

explain.text: The first commit took the staged a.py. The staging area was then empty, so the second command made nothing. Each commit needs something newly staged.
